questions.question_text:
The table shows the distances in kilometres between four towns.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{From/To} & A & B & C & D \\ \hline A & - & 12 & - & 15 \\ B & 12 & - & 8 & 11 \\ C & - & 8 & - & 9 \\ D & 15 & 11 & 9 & - \end{array}$
How many edges are in the network diagram and what is the degree of vertex $B$?

options.why: Counted every symmetric non-dash entry twice rather than counting unique edges.
Included the dash on the leading diagonal in the vertex degree count.
Miscounted non-dash entries in row $B$.

questions.solution_text:
Count unique pairs above the diagonal: $AB=12, AD=15, BC=8, BD=11, CD=9$.
Number of edges $= 5$
Degree of $B$ is the number of connections in row $B$: $3$.
$5$ edges, $\deg(B) = 3$

questions.question_text:
A directed network is given by the table:
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{From/To} & P & Q & R & S \\ \hline P & - & 5 & - & - \\ Q & - & - & 4 & 7 \\ R & 3 & - & - & 2 \\ S & - & - & - & - \end{array}$
Which vertex has the highest **out-degree** (most outgoing edges)?

options.text: Vertices $Q$ and $R$ tie with an out-degree of $2$

options.why: Confused out-degree with in-degree (incoming edges to $S$).
Counted the column entries for $P$ instead of row entries.

options.text: Vertex $Q$ alone with an out-degree of $11$
options.why: Summed edge weights instead of counting the number of outgoing edges.

questions.solution_text:
Out-degree equals the count of non-dash entries in each row:
Row $P$: $1$
Row $Q$: $2$ ($Q\to R, Q\to S$)
Row $R$: $2$ ($R\to P, R\to S$)
Row $S$: $0$
Vertices $Q$ and $R$ tie with out-degree $2$.

questions.question_text: Four office rooms $A, B, C, D$ are connected by corridors. Corridors connect $A\text{–}B$, $A\text{–}C$, $B\text{–}C$, $B\text{–}D$, and $C\text{–}D$. Corridors can be walked in either direction. Which table is the correct adjacency matrix?

options.why: Placed $1$s on the diagonal representing non-existent loops.
Added a corridor between $A$ and $D$ instead of between $B$ and $D$.
Omitted reciprocal entries, treating two-way corridors as one-way.

questions.solution_text:
Corridors are two-way connections ($1$):
$A$ connects to $B, C$.
$B$ connects to $A, C, D$.
$C$ connects to $A, B, D$.
$D$ connects to $B, C$.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} & A & B & C & D \\ \hline A & - & 1 & 1 & - \\ B & 1 & - & 1 & 1 \\ C & 1 & 1 & - & 1 \\ D & - & 1 & 1 & - \end{array}$

questions.question_text: Why does a directed network typically produce an **asymmetric** adjacency matrix?

options.text: A directed edge from $X$ to $Y$ creates an entry in row $X$, column $Y$, but not necessarily in row $Y$, column $X$
Directed networks always contain loops from a vertex to itself
options.why: Directed graphs do not necessarily contain loops.

options.text: The sum of edge weights in a directed graph must always be odd
options.why: There is no requirement that edge weight sums must be odd.

options.text: Vertices in directed graphs cannot have both incoming and outgoing edges
options.why: Vertices in directed graphs routinely have both incoming and outgoing edges.

questions.solution_text:
In a directed graph, an edge from $X$ to $Y$ only allows travel in that direction.
Thus, row $X$, column $Y$ has a weight, but row $Y$, column $X$ remains a dash unless an opposite edge exists.
A directed edge $X\to Y$ creates an entry at $(X,Y)$ but not $(Y,X)$.

questions.question_text:
An undirected network connects four towns $A, B, C, D$ with the distance matrix:
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} \text{From/To} & A & B & C & D \\ \hline A & - & 14 & x & 18 \\ B & 14 & - & 9 & y \\ C & x & 9 & - & 11 \\ D & 18 & y & 11 & - \end{array}$
The network diagram shows edge $AC = 16\text{ km}$ and edge $BD = 13\text{ km}$. What is the value of $x + y$?

options.why: Used $14 + 13 = 27$ by misidentifying edge $AB$ instead of $AC$.
Used $18 + 16 = 34$ by misidentifying edge $AD$ instead of $BD$.
Subtracted $9$ from $29$ instead of summing $x$ and $y$.

questions.question_text:
A directed network connecting five stations $V_1, V_2, V_3, V_4, V_5$ has the adjacency matrix:
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} \text{From/To} & V_1 & V_2 & V_3 & V_4 & V_5 \\ \hline V_1 & - & 8 & 12 & - & - \\ V_2 & - & - & - & 15 & - \\ V_3 & 7 & - & - & 11 & 14 \\ V_4 & - & - & 9 & - & 6 \\ V_5 & - & - & - & - & - \end{array}$
What is the total **outgoing weight** from station $V_3$?

options.why: Summed incoming weights into $V_3$ from column $V_3$ ($12 + 9 = 21$).
Omitted the directed edge $V_3\to V_1$ of weight $7$.
Summed both row $V_3$ and column $V_3$ entries ($32 + 21 = 53$).

questions.solution_text:
Outgoing edges from $V_3$ are the entries in row $V_3$:
$V_3\to V_1 = 7$
$V_3\to V_4 = 11$
$V_3\to V_5 = 14$
$\text{Total outgoing weight} = 7 + 11 + 14$
$= 32$
